hypertrophic-pyloric-stenosis.name: Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis
hypertrophic-pyloric-stenosis.scope: infantile presentation (nonbilious projectile vomiting, olive mass), hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, ultrasound diagnosis, fluid resuscitation, pyloromyotomy
hypertrophic-pyloric-stenosis.core: A hungry young infant with progressive projectile nonbilious vomiting suggests gastric outlet obstruction from pyloric muscle hypertrophy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually 2–8 weeks old; more common in firstborn boys and with family history
Early-life macrolide exposure, especially erythromycin; bottle feeding and maternal smoking associated

rows.label: Clues
items: Vomiting becomes forceful after feeds; dehydration, weight loss, fewer wet diapers
★ **Palpable epigastric/right-upper-quadrant olive**, visible left-to-right gastric peristalsis
★ **Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis** after prolonged vomiting; labs may initially be normal
Bilious emesis is atypical and demands urgent evaluation for obstruction distal to ampulla

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hypertrophied pyloric circular muscle obstructs gastric emptying without blocking bile drainage into distal bowel
Gastric HCl loss and contraction activate aldosterone → renal potassium loss; severe depletion causes paradoxical aciduria

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Ultrasound first**: thickened elongated pylorus with impaired passage
Typical thresholds: muscle thickness ≥3 mm, channel length ≥15 mm; interpret by infant size
Equivocal early study → repeat ultrasound; upper GI series can show string sign if uncertainty persists
Electrolytes, glucose, renal function, blood gas assess resuscitation needs before anesthesia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO + IV isotonic saline**, glucose-containing maintenance fluid; correct chloride deficit first
Replace potassium after confirming urine output; monitor hydration and electrolytes
★ **Pyloromyotomy after normalization** of volume and alkalosis; medical stabilization precedes definitive surgery
NG decompression when ongoing vomiting/distention; postoperative feeds advanced with surgical team

rows.label: Complications
items: Severe dehydration, failure to thrive, prerenal AKI, hypokalemic arrhythmia
Persistent alkalosis increases perioperative apnea risk; surgery can cause mucosal perforation or incomplete myotomy
Brief postoperative emesis can occur; persistent worsening vomiting warrants reassessment

rows.label: Prevention
items: No reliable primary prevention; avoid unnecessary neonatal macrolides, without withholding necessary treatment
Early recognition of progressive vomiting prevents severe electrolyte depletion

rows.label: Mimics
items: Physiologic reflux: effortless small spit-ups, normal growth
Malrotation/volvulus: bilious vomiting, acute illness; urgent upper GI evaluation/surgery
Milk-protein allergy: bloody stools, eczema, feeding intolerance rather than fixed outlet obstruction

hypertrophic-pyloric-stenosis.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric surgery teaching.

iga-vasculitis.name: IgA vasculitis
iga-vasculitis.scope: Palpable purpura, arthritis/arthralgias, abdominal pain, intussusception, renal involvement (hematuria, proteinuria, IgA nephropathy), urinalysis monitoring
iga-vasculitis.core: A child with dependent palpable purpura, joint pain, abdominal pain, and renal findings has IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually children age 3–15 years, often following upper respiratory infection
Adults can develop disease with greater renal morbidity; medications/infections may precede episodes

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Nonthrombocytopenic purpura** over buttocks and lower legs; lesions may begin as urticaria
Ankle/knee arthralgia or arthritis, colicky pain, GI bleeding; abdominal symptoms can precede rash
Microscopic hematuria/proteinuria may be silent; scrotal pain/swelling can occur
★ **Severe episodic pain, vomiting, bloody stool** → evaluate intussusception or bowel ischemia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: IgA-containing immune complexes deposit in small vessels and renal mesangium
Vascular inflammation causes skin hemorrhage, bowel-wall edema, joint symptoms, and glomerular injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Classic presentation → **clinical diagnosis**; CBC/platelets, creatinine, urinalysis, BP at baseline
Quantify urine protein if present; complement generally normal, unlike many immune-complex nephritides
Atypical rash → skin biopsy with leukocytoclastic vasculitis and IgA deposition
Persistent substantial proteinuria, hypertension, or impaired kidney function → nephrology, possible renal biopsy
Acute concerning abdominal symptoms → **ultrasound** for intussusception; location often small bowel

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Most cases → **hydration, rest, acetaminophen**; NSAIDs only without renal impairment/GI bleeding
Severe abdominal/joint symptoms → glucocorticoids after excluding surgical complication
Renal disease: BP/proteinuria control with ACE inhibitor/ARB; severe nephritis → biopsy-directed immunosuppression
Intussusception, ischemia, or perforation → urgent pediatric surgical consultation

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent rash, GI hemorrhage, intussusception; nephritic/nephrotic syndrome, CKD
Long-term prognosis mainly follows renal involvement rather than rash severity

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Serial urinalysis and BP for at least 6 months**, longer with abnormalities
Steroids relieve symptoms but **do not reliably prevent nephritis**; counsel on renal warning signs

rows.label: Mimics
items: ITP: low platelets, mucosal bleeding, no vasculitic joint/renal syndrome
Meningococcemia: toxic febrile illness, rapidly progressive purpura, shock
Isolated IgA nephropathy: renal findings without systemic purpura or abdominal disease

iga-vasculitis.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric rheumatology/nephrology teaching.

increased-intracranial-pressure.name: Increased intracranial pressure
increased-intracranial-pressure.scope: Cushing triad, papilledema, ventriculoperitoneal shunt malfunction, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, herniation syndromes, hyperosmolar therapy
increased-intracranial-pressure.core: Progressive headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness from raised intracranial pressure requires rapid distinction between mass effect, hydrocephalus, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, intracranial bleeding, tumor, cerebral edema, CNS infection, obstructed CSF flow
VP shunt: blockage (most common) or infection; IIH: obesity, reproductive-age women, tetracyclines, retinoids/vitamin A supplements

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning/Valsalva headache, papilledema, diplopia from sixth-nerve palsy; infants may have bulging fontanelle
★ **Cushing triad**: hypertension/widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular respirations; late, compensatory; treat ICP, not BP
Uncal herniation → ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral weakness; tonsillar herniation → respiratory arrest
IIH: pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations; shunt failure: recurrent headache, vomiting, lethargy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed skull volume: excess tissue, blood, or CSF raises pressure after compensatory reserve exhausted
Cerebral perfusion pressure = MAP − ICP; falling perfusion worsens ischemia and edema
IIH: **impaired CSF resorption** at arachnoid granulations; ventricles normal/small, no obstruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unstable/acute deficit → **noncontrast head CT**; papilledema with stable suspected IIH → MRI + MRV
★ **No LP before excluding mass effect/obstructive hydrocephalus** when concerning signs present
IIH: normal imaging aside from supportive findings → **LP**: normal CSF composition, opening pressure ≥25 cm H₂O
Shunt failure → head imaging, shunt series, urgent neurosurgery; normal ventricular size does not exclude obstruction
Recent shunt revision + fever + neutrophilic CSF → **shunt infection**, not community meningitis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Herniation concern → **airway/intubation first**, head elevation, IV **hypertonic saline or mannitol**, urgent neurosurgery
Avoid hypoxia/hypotension; brief controlled hyperventilation only as bridge for impending herniation
Hydrocephalus → CSF drainage/shunt revision; mass lesion → definitive decompression
Dexamethasone for tumor-associated vasogenic edema; no corticosteroids for traumatic brain injury
IIH → weight loss + acetazolamide; threatened vision → optic nerve fenestration or CSF diversion

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent visual loss, ischemic injury, herniation, death
Hyperosmolar agents → electrolyte/renal disturbances; CSF devices → infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid causative drugs in IIH; follow visual fields and optic discs
Shunt education: prompt evaluation for recurrence or fever; injury prevention

rows.label: Mimics
items: Migraine: normal fundus and no progressive focal/mental-status findings
Cerebral venous thrombosis: venous obstruction on MRV, not idiopathic disease

increased-intracranial-pressure.evidence: Not checked online; established neurocritical care and IIH diagnostic principles.

knee-injuries.name: Knee injuries
knee-injuries.scope: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear, posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) tear, collateral ligaments, meniscal tears, knee dislocation, popliteal artery injury, Ottawa knee rules
knee-injuries.core: Knee trauma assessment starts with neurovascular safety and fracture risk, then uses mechanism, effusion timing, and targeted ligament or meniscal tests.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pivoting/cutting sports, contact trauma, dashboard impact, hyperextension
Older age, osteoporosis, and inability to bear weight increase fracture probability

rows.label: Clues
items: Immediate large effusion suggests hemarthrosis; delayed swelling and catching suggest meniscal injury
★ **Gross deformity or spontaneously reduced dislocation** → popliteal artery injury risk
Cool foot, weak pulses, paresthesia, escalating pain → vascular compromise or compartment syndrome

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ligament disruption → instability; displaced meniscal fragment → mechanical locking
Knee dislocation may stretch/tear popliteal artery despite restored alignment and initially palpable pulses

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Neurovascular examination before and after reduction**; ABI assesses arterial injury
★ ABI **<0.9, abnormal pulses, or pre-reduction deficit → CT angiography**; hard ischemic signs → vascular intervention
Normal ABI/pulses, no prior deficit → serial vascular checks, not immediate discharge
Ottawa: age ≥55, isolated patellar/fibular-head tenderness, flexion <90°, or inability four-step weight-bearing → radiographs
MRI for soft-tissue injury after fracture evaluation; locked knee → prompt orthopedic assessment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Dislocation → **urgent reduction before angiography**, immobilization, orthopedic/vascular consultation
Initial sprain → ice/compression, analgesia, protected weight bearing then early rehabilitation
Isolated collateral sprain → hinged brace + rehabilitation; many PCL injuries managed nonoperatively
ACL rupture with athletic demands/persistent instability or combined injury → reconstruction discussion
Displaced locked meniscal tear → arthroscopy; degenerative tears without locking usually exercise-based rehabilitation

rows.label: Complications
items: Missed arterial injury → limb loss; peroneal nerve injury → foot drop
Chronic instability, recurrent meniscal injury, posttraumatic osteoarthritis, stiffness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Neuromuscular landing/pivot training, strength and balance rehabilitation before sport return

rows.label: Mimics
items: Patellar dislocation: lateral patellar displacement, often spontaneous reduction
Septic arthritis: atraumatic hot effusion, fever; urgent aspiration
Patellofemoral pain/instability: running, stairs, sitting → anterior pain; crepitus, genu valgum, lax patella; no effusion unless acute dislocation
Osgood-Schlatter: growth-spurt athlete, chronic tibial tubercle pain; traction apophysitis, tendon-insertion microfractures

table.title: Mechanism and examination
rows: Joint-line tenderness; McMurray: click on rotation/extension; Thessaly

knee-injuries.evidence: Not checked online; established orthopedic trauma and Ottawa knee principles.

lactose-intolerance.name: Lactose intolerance
lactose-intolerance.scope: Primary lactase deficiency, secondary lactase deficiency, hydrogen breath test, stool reducing substances, dietary restriction, lactase replacement
lactose-intolerance.core: Bloating, flatulence and watery diarrhea after lactose ingestion reflect carbohydrate malabsorption rather than milk-protein allergy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Primary lactase nonpersistence increases after childhood and varies by ancestry
Secondary brush-border injury: viral gastroenteritis, celiac disease, Crohn disease, giardiasis
Congenital lactase deficiency rare; preterm infants can have transient developmental enzyme deficiency

rows.label: Clues
items: Dose-related cramps and gas within hours after milk/ice cream; symptoms improve without lactose
Stools lack blood; isolated intolerance does not cause fever or systemic inflammation
Infants with secondary malabsorption may develop acidic diarrhea and perianal irritation
Weight loss, anemia, nocturnal diarrhea or persistent symptoms despite restriction suggest another disorder

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Low intestinal lactase prevents lactose cleavage into absorbable glucose/galactose
Unabsorbed sugar retains luminal water; bacterial fermentation produces hydrogen and organic acids

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symptoms → **lactose elimination and rechallenge**; history often sufficient
★ Uncertain diagnosis → **hydrogen breath test** after lactose; rising hydrogen with symptoms supports intolerance
Stool reducing substances and low pH can support infant carbohydrate malabsorption; limited specificity
Persistent/refractory symptoms → targeted evaluation for celiac disease, giardiasis or other mucosal injury
Distinguish lactose malabsorption on testing from clinically symptomatic intolerance

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Reduce lactose to tolerated amount**; complete lifelong dairy exclusion usually unnecessary
Lactase enzyme with lactose-containing meals or lactose-free dairy; divided portions with food improve tolerance
Yogurt with live cultures and aged hard cheese often tolerated better than milk
★ Maintain **calcium and vitamin D** through tolerated foods, fortified alternatives or supplements
Treat secondary cause; retry lactose after mucosal recovery rather than assuming permanent deficiency

rows.label: Complications
items: Unnecessary dairy restriction → low calcium intake and impaired bone health
Severe infant diarrhea can cause dehydration; uncomplicated adult intolerance does not damage intestinal mucosa

rows.label: Prevention
items: Identify personal threshold; review lactose in foods and maintain nutritionally complete substitutes
Temporary reduced intake after gastroenteritis may help selected persistent cases

rows.label: Mimics
items: Milk-protein allergy: eczema, wheeze, urticaria or bloody infant stools
Celiac disease: nutrient deficiencies and positive tTG-IgA
IBS: broader food/stress triggers, no reproducible lactose-specific pattern

lymphoma.name: Lymphoma
lymphoma.scope: Hodgkin lymphoma (Reed-Sternberg cells, CD15/CD30, B symptoms, mediastinal mass), non-Hodgkin lymphoma (diffuse large B-cell, follicular, Burkitt, mantle cell), Ann Arbor staging, excisional lymph node biopsy
lymphoma.core: Persistent painless lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, or constitutional symptoms require tissue diagnosis; lymphoma subtype determines urgency, staging, and treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: EBV, HIV, transplantation/immunosuppression; autoimmune disease and older age for many NHL subtypes
Hodgkin incidence peaks in young adults and older age

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **B symptoms**: unexplained fever >38 °C, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss in 6 months
Young adult, persistent painless cervical node + **generalized pruritus** → suspect Hodgkin
Rubbery nodes; NHL often noncontiguous/extranodal
Rapidly enlarging mass, cytopenias, high LDH → aggressive disease; mediastinal disease may obstruct airway/SVC

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Clonal lymphocyte proliferation; most NHLs are B-cell derived
Classical Hodgkin: sparse malignant cells within a reactive inflammatory background

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Excisional lymph-node biopsy** preserves architecture; core if excision unsafe; FNA alone generally insufficient
Histology, immunophenotyping/flow cytometry, selected cytogenetics classify disease; PET/CT stages FDG-avid lymphoma
Ann Arbor: I one region; II same diaphragm side; III both sides; IV disseminated extranodal disease
CBC, CMP, LDH, uric acid; HIV/HBV/HCV testing before systemic treatment
Stable before biopsy → avoid glucocorticoids obscuring histology; life-threatening compression → urgent specialist management

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Early classical HL → **ABVD ± involved-site radiation**; advanced disease → nivolumab-AVD among current options
DLBCL → rituximab-based combination, commonly R-CHOP; Burkitt → urgent intensive chemotherapy with CNS-directed treatment
Asymptomatic low-burden follicular disease → observation; symptomatic/bulky disease → anti-CD20-based treatment
★ Assess tumor-lysis risk before cytotoxic treatment; hydration and **urate-lowering prophylaxis** when risk warrants

rows.label: Complications
items: Tumor lysis, marrow failure, infection, cord compression, superior vena cava syndrome
Doxorubicin → cardiomyopathy; bleomycin → lung toxicity; later infertility/secondary cancers

rows.label: Prevention
items: Anti-CD20 plus HBsAg+ or anti-HBc+ → entecavir/tenofovir prophylaxis; fertility preservation before chemotherapy
Survivorship care: cardiovascular risk, thyroid/breast surveillance after relevant radiation exposures

rows.label: Mimics
items: Reactive nodes: tender, infection-linked, regress after illness
TB lymphadenitis: granulomatous inflammation; microbiologic confirmation
Leukemia: circulating blasts or marked blood-count abnormalities; marrow evaluation

neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.name: Neonatal intestinal obstruction
neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.scope: Malrotation with midgut volvulus, duodenal atresia, jejunoileal atresia, meconium ileus, Hirschsprung disease, bilious vomiting, upper GI contrast series, Ladd procedure
neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.core: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is intestinal obstruction until proved otherwise; volvulus must be excluded before bowel ischemia develops.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Polyhydramnios → prenatal proximal obstruction; Down syndrome → duodenal atresia
CF → meconium ileus; trisomy 21 → Hirschsprung disease
Prematurity increases alternative risk of necrotizing enterocolitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Proximal obstruction → early vomiting with little distention; distal obstruction → marked distention
No meconium by **48 hours**, explosive stool after rectal exam → distal aganglionosis
★ Bloody stool, tenderness, shock or metabolic acidosis → ischemic bowel; urgent surgery
Volvulus: sudden bilious emesis after normal feeding and meconium; atresia: vomiting from first feeds

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Malrotation leaves narrow mesenteric base → twisting of bowel and mesenteric blood supply
Duodenal atresia: failed recanalization; jejunoileal atresia: fetal vascular injury
Hirschsprung: absent enteric ganglia → failure of distal relaxation and proximal dilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal radiograph** first; double bubble without distal gas supports duodenal atresia
★ Suspected malrotation, stable → **upper GI contrast series**; corkscrew/abnormal DJ junction; enema: misplaced cecum
Distal obstruction → contrast enema to characterize microcolon, meconium or transition zone
Hirschsprung confirmation → **rectal suction biopsy**, absent ganglion cells
Peritonitis or unstable suspected volvulus → exploration without delaying for contrast

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ All suspected obstruction → **NPO, orogastric decompression, IV fluids**, pediatric surgery
Volvulus → emergency Ladd procedure, detorsion and viability assessment; broad antibiotics if ischemic
Atresias → operative repair after stabilization; duodenal repair commonly duodenoduodenostomy
Uncomplicated meconium ileus → water-soluble contrast enema with hydration; complicated cases → surgery
Hirschsprung → irrigations then pull-through; enterocolitis → fluids, decompression, IV broad antibiotics

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis, short-bowel syndrome; Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis can be fatal
Delayed diagnosis causes aspiration, electrolyte depletion and growth failure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pyloric stenosis: nonbilious projectile emesis at several weeks
NEC: ill preterm infant, pneumatosis intestinalis
Physiologic reflux: thriving infant without bile or distention

table.title: Distal obstruction clues
rows: Narrow distal segment, proximal transition zone

newborn-screening.name: Newborn screening
newborn-screening.scope: Congenital hypothyroidism (macroglossia, umbilical hernia, levothyroxine), phenylketonuria, galactosemia, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, hemoglobinopathies, cystic fibrosis, pulse oximetry, hearing screen
newborn-screening.core: Screen apparently healthy newborns for treatable metabolic, endocrine, genetic, cardiac, and hearing disorders before symptoms or irreversible injury.

rows.label: Who
items: All newborns; blood-spot panels vary by state; also screen cardiac oxygenation and hearing

rows.label: Start/stop
items: ★ Heel stick **24–48 hours**; early collection, transfusion, prematurity may require repeats
Pulse oximetry ≥24 hours or before early discharge; hearing by 1 month

rows.label: Test
items: ★ Cardiac pass: **≥95% in both right hand and foot**, difference ≤3 percentage points
<90% anywhere → immediate failure; otherwise **one repeat** in 1 hour (older algorithms: two)
Hearing: otoacoustic emissions or auditory brainstem response; NICU → brainstem-based screen

rows.label: IF positive
items: ★ Critical result → confirm promptly without delaying lifesaving treatment
Failed cardiac screen → evaluate hypoxemia, echocardiography; ductal-dependent lesion → prostaglandin E1
★ Failed hearing → diagnostic audiology by **3 months**, intervention by **6 months**

rows.label: Traps
items: Normal examination does not exclude disease; hypothyroidism later causes macroglossia/umbilical hernia
Ill infant with suspected CAH → treat despite pending screen; no diagnostic reassurance
Hereditary fructose intolerance: symptoms only after fructose/sucrose, so not on breast milk alone

table.title: Urgent positive blood-spot results
rows: Start levothyroxine promptly, ideally by 2 weeks
Classic galactosemia: feeding → vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly
Penicillin from infancy, vaccines, hematology follow-up
Specialty care, nutrition, pancreatic enzymes if insufficient

newborn-screening.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [CDC cardiac screening](https://www.cdc.gov/heart-defects/hcp/screening/), [CDC hearing](https://www.cdc.gov/hearing-loss-children/screening/); blood-spot actions established teaching.

parasitic-infections.name: Parasitic infections
parasitic-infections.scope: Strongyloidiasis, giardiasis, amebiasis, cryptosporidiosis, ascariasis, schistosomiasis, pinworm (enterobiasis), cysticercosis, eosinophilia workup, antiparasitic therapy
parasitic-infections.core: Exposure, organ pattern, and immune status identify the parasite; eosinophilia favors tissue-invasive helminths rather than intestinal protozoa.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Contaminated food/water, endemic travel, freshwater contact, barefoot soil exposure, household crowding
Steroids/HTLV-1 predispose to Strongyloides hyperinfection; advanced HIV predisposes to persistent cryptosporidiosis

rows.label: Clues
items: Ascariasis: transient cough/eosinophilic infiltrates during larval migration; later intestinal or biliary obstruction
Pinworm: nocturnal perianal/vulvar itch, dysuria with normal UA; household clustering
Cysticercosis: seizures or hydrocephalus; ingestion of **T. solium eggs**, not pork cysts
Cutaneous larva migrans: soil contact; pruritic **serpiginous tracks**; animal hookworm larvae → albendazole or ivermectin

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Giardia blunts microvilli → **fat/carbohydrate malabsorption**; invasive protozoa can affect liver, urinary tract, or CNS
Strongyloides autoinfection permits lifelong persistence and dissemination after immunosuppression

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unexplained **eosinophilia** → travel/drug history, serial stool O&P, targeted Strongyloides serology
★ Steroids + eosinophilia or infiltrates → **Strongyloides hyperinfection**: **duodenal aspirate** larvae; stool O&P often misses
Diarrhea → stool antigen/PCR for protozoa; single routine O&P can miss infection
★ Pinworm → **morning tape test** before washing; stool testing insensitive
Brain MRI/CT for cysticercosis; eye examination before antiparasitics; assess lesion viability and location

rows.label: Tx
items: Rehydrate; ascariasis → albendazole; bowel obstruction → surgical evaluation before deworming
Pinworm → albendazole, mebendazole, or pyrantel; repeat after **2 weeks**, treat household simultaneously
★ Viable parenchymal cysticercosis → albendazole ± praziquantel with corticosteroids; seizures → levetiracetam
Calcified brain lesions → no antiparasitic; hydrocephalus → neurosurgical control before cysticidal treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Strongyloides hyperinfection → gram-negative sepsis, respiratory failure; eosinophilia may disappear
Amebic liver abscess; schistosomiasis → portal hypertension or bladder squamous carcinoma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Screen/treat Strongyloides before **immunosuppression** after endemic exposure
Safe water, sanitation, handwashing, footwear; avoid endemic freshwater and untreated swimming water
Neurocysticercosis household contacts → **stool O&P** to find egg-shedding T. solium tapeworm carrier

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBD: chronic inflammatory diarrhea after infection excluded
Drug hypersensitivity: eosinophilia linked to new medication, rash or organ injury

table.title: Exposure → diagnosis and treatment
rows: Camping; greasy stool, bloating; stool antigen
Dysentery, flask-shaped ulcers; stool PCR; abscess → serology
Soil; larva currens, larvae in stool
Ivermectin; hyperinfection requires prolonged daily treatment
Freshwater; hematuria (haematobium), portal fibrosis (mansoni/japonicum); eggs, serology
Confirmed E. histolytica without invasive disease

parasomnias.name: Parasomnias
parasomnias.scope: REM sleep behavior disorder (polysomnography, clonazepam), sleep terrors, sleepwalking (somnambulism), nightmare disorder, isolated sleep paralysis, reassurance
parasomnias.core: Unusual behavior or experiences during sleep are classified by timing, recall, and whether REM muscle atonia is lost or persists.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sleep deprivation, stress, fever, alcohol, OSA precipitate NREM arousals
REM behavior disorder: older men, synucleinopathies, SSRIs; sleepwalking/terrors often childhood

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Dream enactment with injury** → ask bed partner about kicking, punching, falling from bed
Isolated sleep paralysis: conscious but briefly unable to move at sleep onset or awakening

rows.label: Pathophys
items: NREM disorders: incomplete arousal from deep sleep; REM behavior disorder: loss of normal skeletal atonia
Sleep paralysis: REM atonia persists into wakefulness

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected REM behavior disorder → **video polysomnography** demonstrating REM without atonia
Typical childhood NREM events: clinical; atypical stereotyped episodes → video EEG/PSG
Assess snoring, sleep schedule, drugs, trauma, daytime sleep attacks

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ REM behavior disorder: **immediate-release melatonin or clonazepam**; melatonin favored with falls/OSA concerns
Sleep terrors/walking: reassurance, adequate sleep, scheduled awakenings for predictable frequent events
Nightmares: imagery rehearsal; trauma-associated nightmares → assess PTSD
Isolated paralysis: reassurance, regular sleep; accompanying cataplexy → evaluate narcolepsy

rows.label: Complications
items: Injury to sleeper/partner; clonazepam can worsen sedation, balance, sleep-disordered breathing
REM behavior disorder may precede Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia, or multiple system atrophy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Safe bedroom**: remove weapons, pad furniture, secure windows; separate sleeping if violent
Avoid sleep deprivation/alcohol; treat OSA; review triggering antidepressants

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nocturnal seizures: brief stereotyped clusters, possible postictal findings
OSA: gasping arousals tied to obstructive respiratory events

table.title: Timing and recall
rows: Awake, oriented, detailed frightening dream recall

pediatric-hip-disorders.name: Pediatric hip disorders
pediatric-hip-disorders.scope: Developmental dysplasia of the hip, Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, transient synovitis, pediatric limp workup
pediatric-hip-disorders.core: A child’s limp or knee pain may originate in the hip; age, weight-bearing ability, and hip rotation separate common developmental disorders.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Breech presentation, female sex, family history → developmental hip dysplasia
Obesity and adolescence → slipped capital femoral epiphysis; atypically young/thin cases suggest endocrine disease
Recent viral illness → transient synovitis; Perthes often boys aged 4–8 years

rows.label: Clues
items: Infant asymmetric abduction or leg length; older child limp, groin/thigh/knee pain
★ **Fever, toxic appearance, refusal to bear weight**, painful restricted motion → septic arthritis concern
SCFE: obligate external rotation with flexion, limited internal rotation/abduction; Perthes: gradual painless/painful limp with limited internal rotation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysplasia: shallow acetabulum and unstable femoral head; Perthes: femoral-head avascular necrosis
SCFE: physeal failure displaces epiphysis relative to neck; synovitis: transient sterile joint inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Examine hip in unexplained knee pain**: gait, rotation, fever; limited rotation → **hip x-ray**, not knee MRI
DDH: Ortolani reduces dislocation; Barlow provokes instability; limited abduction more useful after early infancy
Risk-based DDH imaging → ultrasound around 6 weeks; radiograph after femoral ossification, usually ≥4–6 months
Suspected septic hip → CBC, ESR/CRP, cultures, ultrasound for effusion → urgent aspiration
Kocher features: fever >38.5°C, nonweight-bearing, WBC >12,000, ESR >40; support concern, never replace aspiration

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected SCFE → **immediate nonweight-bearing**, orthopedic fixation; no forceful manipulation
★ Septic joint → **urgent drainage + IV antibiotics** after cultures when feasible
Transient synovitis → rest, NSAID, close reassessment; persistent/worsening symptoms require renewed evaluation
Perthes → orthopedic containment/ROM plan; DDH treatment depends on age and stability below

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated dysplasia → early osteoarthritis; SCFE → avascular necrosis/chondrolysis
Perthes → femoral-head deformity; missed septic arthritis → irreversible joint destruction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Newborn and infant hip examinations; avoid tight swaddling with extended adducted hips

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomyelitis: focal bony tenderness, MRI marrow changes
Trauma: injury history and fracture imaging

table.title: Imaging and definitive branch
rows: Sclerosis, flattening, fragmentation; decreased bone-scan uptake

pediatric-hip-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric orthopedic assessment principles.

pediculosis.name: Pediculosis
pediculosis.scope: Pediculosis capitis (head lice), pediculosis corporis, phthiriasis pubis (pubic lice), topical permethrin, malathion, environmental control, contact management
pediculosis.core: Pruritic ectoparasite infestation confirmed by identifying lice or viable eggs; treatment must address the organism's habitat and exposed contacts.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Head-to-head contact in children; sexual contact for pubic infestation; crowding/limited clean clothing for body infestation
Head lice unrelated to poor hygiene; human lice do not jump, fly, or come from pets

rows.label: Clues
items: Scalp itching, excoriations, occipital nodes; eggs firmly attached rather than loosely flaking
Body infestation: truncal excoriations along clothing contact; pubic infestation may cause blue-gray macules

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Blood-feeding arthropods; salivary antigens induce delayed pruritus; eggs survive some adulticidal treatments

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Live crawling louse** confirms active infestation; wet-combing and magnification improve detection
Nits alone, especially distant from scalp, may reflect old infection; no routine laboratory tests
★ Pubic lice → test **HIV, syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia**; assess sexual exposure history

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Resistant head lice → **spinosad or topical ivermectin**; malathion alternative at age ≥6 years
Malathion **flammable**: no hair dryer/flames; avoid lindane because of neurotoxicity
★ Check household members; treat infested contacts and **bed-sharing contacts simultaneously**
Pubic infestation: treat sexual partners from prior month; abstain until everyone treated
Eyelash involvement → ophthalmic petrolatum, specialist removal; no routine pediculicide near eyes

rows.label: Complications
items: Scratching → impetigo; body lice transmit epidemic typhus, trench fever, louse-borne relapsing fever
Persistent itching alone after treatment does not establish resistance; look for surviving organisms

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Wash recently used bedding/clothes at **≥130°F**, hot dry; unwashable items → sealed bag 2 weeks
Clean combs; vacuum upholstered surfaces; avoid shared headwear; no household insecticide fogging
Children may return after starting treatment; no-nit exclusion policies unnecessary

rows.label: Mimics
items: Dandruff: flakes slide off hair; nits cemented to shaft
Scabies: nocturnal itch, finger-web burrows; lice visible on hair/clothes

table.title: Habitat and first treatment
rows: Bathing, clean clothing, laundering; pediculicide rarely needed

physician-patient-communication.name: Physician-patient communication
physician-patient-communication.scope: Medical interpreters, limited English proficiency, delivering bad news, empathetic communication, family requests to withhold information
physician-patient-communication.core: Respect autonomy through understandable, honest, empathic dialogue; identify what patients understand and want before sharing decisions or sensitive information.

rows.label: Principle
items: Confidentiality, cultural humility, informed choice; language barriers never imply impaired capacity
Patient preferences determine family involvement and desired level of disclosure
**Comprehensive, contextual care**: whole-person, longitudinal; tailored to culture, family, goals

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Qualified medical interpreter**, free to patient; speak directly to patient in short segments
★ Bad news: privacy → understanding/preferences → warning → plain disclosure → empathy → plan
Validate emotion; open questions, silence, teach-back; explore beliefs before correcting misinformation

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid jargon, false reassurance, interrupting, arguing, blaming, or premature advice
Avoid routine reliance on children/family for interpreting consent or sensitive discussions
Avoid promising cure or confidentiality beyond legal limits

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ **Family requests nondisclosure → ask patient privately**; patient preferences control disclosure
Capable patient may decline details or designate another recipient; document preference
Emergency without interpreter → temporary available help while securing qualified interpretation

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Therapeutic privilege is narrow**; anticipated distress alone never justifies withholding diagnosis
Anger → acknowledge concern, clarify cause, establish boundaries if threatening; no reflex discharge
Requested adult-family interpreter → verify suitability/privacy/voluntariness; offer professional

table.title: Difficult conversations
rows: Pause; allow feelings; schedule prompt follow-up
Voice openly in patient's presence; no covert action
Capable patient hides news from family
Encourage support; respect privacy; never lie to family
Child asks prognosis, parents forbid disclosure
Explore understanding; encourage talking with parents; never lie
Negotiate adherence contract; punitive control backfires
Fluent bilingual staff acceptable; never a child

primary-immunodeficiencies.name: Primary immunodeficiencies
primary-immunodeficiencies.scope: Selective IgA deficiency, common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), X-linked agammaglobulinemia, severe combined immunodeficiency, hyper-IgE syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich, chronic granulomatous disease
primary-immunodeficiencies.core: Recurrent, unusually severe, persistent, or opportunistic infections; organism pattern and age of onset localize the immune defect.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Consanguinity, affected relatives, male relatives dying in infancy; absent family history does not exclude disease

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, persistent thrush, or infections across multiple organ systems
Deep abscesses suggest phagocyte dysfunction; recurrent encapsulated bacteria suggest impaired antibody function

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Selective IgA deficiency: impaired mucosal defense; respiratory infections, giardiasis, atopy, or no symptoms
Antibody disorders impair opsonization; T-cell defects permit viral, fungal, and protozoal opportunists
DiGeorge: 3rd/4th **pharyngeal pouch** failure → absent thymus, hypocalcemia, conotruncal defects, T-cell infections
ADA deficiency: autosomal recessive SCID; toxic deoxyadenosine destroys T and B cells

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Start **CBC with differential, quantitative immunoglobulins**, HIV testing; assess vaccine antibody responses
Lymphocyte subsets distinguish B-cell and T-cell deficiencies; abnormal results → genetic confirmation
IgA deficiency: isolated IgA <7 mg/dL after age 4 years; normal IgG and IgM
★ Newborn **TREC screen** detects impaired T-cell production before symptomatic SCID

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Profound combined immune failure → isolation, irradiated CMV-negative blood products, urgent **transplant evaluation**
Acute infections: organism-directed antimicrobials; immunoglobulin replacement not useful for isolated IgA deficiency

rows.label: Complications
items: Bronchiectasis, chronic enteropathy, autoimmune disease; CVID additionally increases lymphoma risk
Anti-IgA antibodies can cause anaphylaxis to blood products

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Avoid **live vaccines** in major T-cell defects; immunize household contacts with safe vaccine choices
IgA-related transfusion reactions → washed cellular products or IgA-deficient plasma
CGD: TMP-SMX + itraconazole prophylaxis; genetic counseling for inherited defects

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vertical HIV: bacterial infections + zoster, nodes, maternal opportunistic infection; low CD4, positive virologic testing
Secondary hypogammaglobulinemia: nephrotic protein loss, B-cell malignancy, or rituximab exposure

table.title: Defect fingerprints
rows: Adolescent/adult; low IgG, poor vaccine response
Boy after 6 months; absent tonsils/B cells
Infant; absent thymic shadow, profound lymphopenia
Cold abscesses, eczema, retained teeth, pneumatoceles

scabies.name: Scabies
scabies.scope: Sarcoptes scabiei infestation, pruritus worse at night, burrows in web spaces and flexures, mineral oil scraping, topical permethrin, oral ivermectin, household contact treatment
scabies.core: Contagious mite infestation causing intense nocturnal itching, especially when household members also itch; eradicate infestation and treat exposed contacts simultaneously.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prolonged skin contact, sexual exposure, crowded households, nursing facilities
Immunosuppression, neurologic impairment, advanced age → crusted disease with enormous mite burden

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Burrows in finger webs**, flexor wrists, axillae, waist, genitalia; excoriated papules/nodules
Adults usually spare head; infants may involve scalp, face, palms and soles
Crusted form: widespread hyperkeratotic plaques, sometimes little pruritus; highly infectious through skin scales

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Sarcoptes scabiei females burrow into stratum corneum; delayed hypersensitivity to mite products produces symptoms
First infestation may remain asymptomatic for weeks; reinfestation causes faster symptoms

rows.label: Dx
items: Typical distribution/contact history → clinical diagnosis; treatment need not await microscopic confirmation
★ **Mineral-oil skin scraping** of burrow → mites, eggs, or feces; negative scraping cannot exclude
Dermoscopy may reveal triangular mite at end of burrow

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Permethrin 5%** neck down, including folds/nails; wash after 8–14 hours; repeat in 1 week
Infants/young children: include scalp/neck; avoid eyes/mouth; sulfur alternative for infants <2 months
Oral ivermectin alternative: two treatments 7–14 days apart; avoid during pregnancy or weight <15 kg
★ Crusted disease → **oral ivermectin + repeated topical permethrin**, keratolytics and contact isolation
Residual itch may last weeks → topical corticosteroid/antihistamine; new burrows prompt reassessment for reinfestation

rows.label: Complications
items: Secondary impetigo/cellulitis from scratching; poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis after infected lesions
Institutional outbreaks; persistent genital nodules may reflect hypersensitivity rather than living mites

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Treat household and sexual contacts simultaneously**, even without symptoms
Hot wash/dry recently used clothing and bedding; bag unwashable items for at least 72 hours
Avoid close skin contact until treatment completed; no insecticide fumigation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Atopic dermatitis: chronic flexural eczema, no burrows or household cluster
Bedbugs: exposed-skin grouped bites, environmental insects; no burrowing
Contact dermatitis: exposure-shaped eruption; contacts usually unaffected

scrotal-masses.name: Scrotal masses
scrotal-masses.scope: Varicocele, hydrocele, spermatocele, testicular cancer differential, physical examination, scrotal Doppler ultrasound
scrotal-masses.core: Painless scrotal swelling requires localization: solid intratesticular lesions are malignant until proven otherwise; many extratesticular lesions are benign.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Testicular cancer: cryptorchidism, prior cancer, family history, younger adult age
Hydrocele: infancy/patent processus vaginalis, trauma, infection; varicocele from venous drainage anatomy

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Firm nontransilluminating intratesticular mass** → urgent malignancy assessment
Dull ache/heaviness may occur without acute inflammation; gynecomastia suggests hormone-secreting germ-cell tumor
New isolated right-sided varicocele or failure to decompress supine → evaluate retroperitoneal obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Patent processus vaginalis permits peritoneal-scrotal communication; epididymal duct obstruction forms retention cysts
Pampiniform venous reflux raises local temperature, potentially impairing spermatogenesis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Nonclassic or possibly solid mass → **scrotal Doppler ultrasound**: intra-/extratesticular location, blood flow
Classic left varicocele on examination → clinical diagnosis; **no imaging**
Examine standing/supine, with Valsalva; determine whether testis separately palpable and mass transilluminates
Suspected tumor → AFP, beta-hCG, LDH before surgery; staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis as needed
Normal markers do not exclude malignancy; AFP elevation excludes pure seminoma

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspicious testicular mass → **radical inguinal orchiectomy**; avoid transscrotal biopsy
Offer sperm banking before cancer treatment; subsequent surveillance/chemotherapy/radiation depends on histology/stage
Newborn transilluminating hydrocele → routine follow-up, usually resolves within 12 months; no aspiration or imaging
Small asymptomatic hydrocele/spermatocele → observe; persistent symptomatic → elective repair
★ Varicocele with **infertility and abnormal semen**, pain, or adolescent testicular atrophy → consider repair

rows.label: Complications
items: Infertility, testicular atrophy; cancer metastasis to retroperitoneal nodes/lungs
Hydrocele may obscure tumor; treatment can impair fertility or endocrine function

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Orchiopexy for undescended testis** reduces infertility risk and facilitates examination; cancer risk persists
No routine population ultrasound or tumor-marker screening; promptly evaluate any new mass

rows.label: Mimics
items: Torsion: sudden severe pain, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex → urgent exploration
Inguinal hernia: reducible groin-continuous swelling, cough impulse
Epididymitis: tender posterior swelling, urinary/STI findings, increased Doppler flow

table.title: Benign examination patterns
rows: Bag of worms; enlarges standing/Valsalva, decompresses supine
Cyst above/behind testis; separate, often transilluminates

scrotal-masses.evidence: Not checked online; established urologic localization and cancer-evaluation principles.

shock.name: Shock
shock.scope: Hypovolemic, cardiogenic, distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic), obstructive, fluid resuscitation, vasopressors
shock.core: Circulatory failure causing tissue hypoperfusion; normal blood pressure does not exclude early shock.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hemorrhage, GI losses, MI, infection, allergen exposure, spinal injury, thromboembolism
Recent surgery, immunosuppression, indwelling devices increase occult infection risk
Procedure bleeding: thoracentesis → intercostal artery, hemothorax; splenectomy → hemoperitoneum, left shoulder pain

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachycardia, altered mentation, oliguria, cool mottled skin; distributive forms may initially feel warm
★ **Anaphylaxis**: rapid airway swelling, wheezing, hypotension; skin findings may be absent
Neurogenic: **lost sympathetic tone** → hypotension, bradycardia or no tachycardia, warm skin after spinal cord injury

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Oxygen delivery falls below demand → anaerobic metabolism, lactate accumulation
Distributive vasodilation → relative hypovolemia despite normal total body fluid
Warm sepsis: high output, **high mixed venous O2**; pump failure: low contractility, congestion; hypovolemia: low preload

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Bedside ultrasound**: cardiac function, pericardial fluid, RV dilation, lung sliding, volume assessment
**Serial lactate**: hypoperfusion, best predicts course and mortality; trend with capillary refill, urine output
Septic shock: vasopressors for MAP ≥65 plus lactate >2 despite volume resuscitation
CBC, chemistry, ECG, troponin; cultures if infection suspected

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway, IV access; **isotonic crystalloid** (balanced, 0.9% saline) before imaging; restrict with pulmonary congestion
★ Hemorrhage → **control bleeding + blood products** (emergency O-negative); crystalloid as bridge; no vasopressors
★ Septic shock → antibiotics within 1 hour, drainage/debridement; crystalloid 30 mL/kg within 3 hours
★ Persistent septic hypotension → **norepinephrine**, MAP ≥65; add vasopressin, then epinephrine; refractory → hydrocortisone
Pulmonary edema after fluids → stop boluses, **inotrope**; children: epinephrine preferred, older exams may expect dopamine

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, ischemic hepatitis, DIC, ARDS, bowel ischemia, multiorgan failure
Excess fluids → edema; vasopressors → digital/mesenteric ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early infection treatment, catheter hygiene, VTE prophylaxis, hemorrhage control
After anaphylaxis: trigger avoidance, epinephrine autoinjector, allergy referral

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vasovagal syncope: transient bradycardia, rapid recovery supine
Hypoglycemia: low bedside glucose, improvement with dextrose
Isolated head injury: hypertension + bradycardia (Cushing); trauma hypotension + tachycardia → assume hemorrhage

table.title: Hemodynamics and cause-directed rescue
rows: Decompress pneumothorax; drain tamponade; reperfuse PE

status-epilepticus.name: Status epilepticus
status-epilepticus.scope: Generalized convulsive status epilepticus, first-line benzodiazepines, second-line antiepileptics, refractory status, reversible causes
status-epilepticus.core: Generalized convulsive seizure lasting ≥5 minutes, or recurrent seizures without recovery between them: treat immediately while seeking reversible causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Missed antiseizure medication, alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal, acute stroke, hemorrhage, tumor, CNS infection
Hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia; stimulant or isoniazid toxicity; eclampsia

rows.label: Clues
items: Bilateral tonic-clonic activity, impaired consciousness, cyanosis, autonomic activation
★ Convulsions stop but consciousness fails to improve → suspect **nonconvulsive status**, not simply sedation
Subtle eye deviation, eyelid/facial twitching may be the only visible ongoing seizure activity

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Sustained excitation and diminishing inhibitory responsiveness → neuronal injury, hypermetabolism, treatment resistance
Hypoxia and systemic metabolic derangements amplify brain injury as seizure duration increases

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Bedside glucose immediately**; electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, renal/liver tests, drug levels, toxicology when relevant
Head CT after stabilization for new focal signs, trauma, or unexplained first episode
★ Persistent impaired awareness/refractory seizure → **continuous EEG**; imaging never delays anticonvulsants
Fever/meningismus → blood cultures, empiric antimicrobials; LP after stabilization and mass-effect assessment

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway, oxygen, suction, IV/IO access; hypoglycemia → dextrose; malnutrition → thiamine without delaying glucose
★ **IV lorazepam** first; no IV access → **IM midazolam**; repeat benzodiazepine once if needed
★ Persistent seizure → IV loading **levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate**; similar second-line efficacy
Benzodiazepine + second-line failure → intubation, ICU, propofol or midazolam infusion guided by continuous EEG
Eclampsia → magnesium; severe hyponatremia → hypertonic saline; isoniazid → pyridoxine; withdrawal → benzodiazepines

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, hypoxic brain injury, rhabdomyolysis, lactic acidosis, hyperthermia; arrhythmias and death
Sedatives → respiratory depression/hypotension; fosphenytoin → arrhythmia; valproate → hepatotoxicity/hyperammonemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication adherence, rescue seizure plan, treatment of precipitating disease; supervised sedative/alcohol withdrawal
Maintain antiseizure therapy before anesthetic withdrawal; driving restrictions, seizure precautions

rows.label: Mimics
items: Psychogenic nonepileptic events: video-EEG lacks ictal correlate; do not diagnose from one bedside sign
Convulsive syncope: brief jerks with rapid recovery; cardiovascular trigger
Postictal state: gradually improving awareness; EEG excludes ongoing electrical seizures when uncertain

stridor.name: Stridor
stridor.scope: Laryngomalacia (inspiratory, worse supine), tracheomalacia (expiratory), vocal cord dysfunction (paradoxical adduction), vascular ring (biphasic, dysphagia), flexible laryngoscopy
stridor.core: Harsh upper-airway noise: respiratory phase localizes obstruction; age, feeding difficulty, and episodic triggers identify the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Congenital airway abnormalities in infancy; prematurity, prior intubation, tracheoesophageal fistula → tracheal weakness
Exercise, stress, irritants → inducible laryngeal obstruction; aortic arch anomalies → extrinsic compression

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Retractions, cyanosis, apnea, exhaustion, or poor air movement** → impending respiratory failure
Feeding-associated choking, recurrent pneumonia, or poor growth → clinically significant obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inspiratory: extrathoracic collapse; expiratory: intrathoracic collapse; biphasic: fixed central obstruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stable unexplained upper-airway noise → **awake flexible laryngoscopy**
Dynamic bronchoscopy assesses distal collapse; CT angiography/MR angiography delineates vascular compression
Normal examination between episodes does not exclude inducible obstruction; visualize during symptoms/exercise
Flow-volume loop: flattened inspiratory limb supports variable extrathoracic obstruction; not definitive alone

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Distress → oxygen, minimize agitation, **urgent controlled airway** with anesthesia/ENT
Mild congenital malacia → observation, feeding assessment, upright feeding while awake; spontaneous improvement with growth
★ Severe laryngeal collapse with apnea/poor growth → **supraglottoplasty**
Severe tracheal collapse → CPAP; refractory disease → airway surgery
Inducible obstruction → speech-guided breathing; symptomatic vascular ring → surgical division

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoxemia, aspiration, recurrent respiratory infections, growth failure; severe obstruction → arrest
Misdiagnosed inducible obstruction → unnecessary bronchodilators, glucocorticoids, or intubations

rows.label: Prevention
items: Supine sleep on flat surface despite positional noise; no prone sleeping or wedges
Avoid smoke exposure; swallowing assessment and feeding modifications reduce aspiration

rows.label: Mimics
items: Croup: acute barky cough after URI; responds to dexamethasone
Foreign body: abrupt choking; rigid bronchoscopy despite normal radiograph
Epiglottitis: fever, drooling, tripod posture; avoid upsetting child or bedside throat examination

table.title: Chronic or episodic causes
rows: Expiratory; barking cough, worsens with exertion
Biphasic wheeze, dysphagia; steroid-unresponsive; neck extension relieves

supraventricular-tachycardia.name: Supraventricular tachycardia
supraventricular-tachycardia.scope: AVNRT, AVRT, focal atrial tachycardia, vagal maneuvers, adenosine, synchronized cardioversion, catheter ablation
supraventricular-tachycardia.core: Abrupt rapid regular palpitations with a usually narrow QRS often represent AV-node-dependent reentry; stability determines immediate electrical versus pharmacologic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Accessory pathway, prior episodes, adrenergic triggers, caffeine/stimulants
Focal atrial tachycardia may accompany structural disease; incessant forms can cause cardiomyopathy

rows.label: Clues
items: Regular rate often 150–250/min; palpitations, lightheadedness, dyspnea, neck pounding
★ **Hypotension, shock, ischemic chest pain, altered mentation**, or acute HF → unstable tachycardia
WPW between episodes: short PR, delta wave, widened QRS; may be absent with concealed pathway

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reentry requires distinct conduction/refractory properties; AV node participates in AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT
Adenosine transiently blocks AV conduction; automatic atrial rhythms may continue despite transient ventricular slowing

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **12-lead ECG during episode**, continuous rhythm monitoring; check electrolytes, medication/exposure triggers
Wide-complex rhythm uncertain → presume VT rather than casually applying narrow-complex algorithm
Structural concern → echocardiography; recurrent undocumented events → ambulatory monitoring/electrophysiology evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable with pulse → **synchronized cardioversion**; sedation if feasible without delaying rescue
★ Stable regular narrow rhythm → **modified Valsalva → rapid IV adenosine**
Persistent stable SVT → IV diltiazem/verapamil or beta blocker if no contraindication; cardioversion if unsuccessful
★ Irregular wide preexcited AF → **procainamide or cardioversion**; avoid AV-nodal blockers, including adenosine
Recurrent symptomatic AVNRT/AVRT or focal tachycardia → catheter ablation; selected patients use oral nodal blockers

rows.label: Complications
items: Syncope, demand ischemia, tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy; preexcited AF can degenerate to VF
Adenosine: brief flushing/chest pressure, bronchospasm; avoid in active severe bronchospasm

rows.label: Prevention
items: Teach vagal maneuver, limit personal triggers; discuss definitive ablation for recurrence
Ablation near AV node carries small heart-block risk; shared procedural decision

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sinus tachycardia: gradual rate changes, beat-to-beat variability, physiologic driver; infants rarely >220/min
Atrial flutter: atrial sawtooth waves, often ventricular rate near 150

supraventricular-tachycardia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [AHA adult advanced life support](https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support), [ACC/AHA AF guideline (2023)](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2023.08.017).

tick-borne-diseases.name: Tick-borne diseases
tick-borne-diseases.scope: Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, babesiosis, anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis, doxycycline therapy
tick-borne-diseases.core: Outdoor exposure followed by multisystem illness: use rash pattern, blood counts, smear and cardiac/neurologic findings to distinguish vector-borne pathogens.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Northeast/upper Midwest Ixodes: Lyme, Babesia, Anaplasma; coinfection possible
Southeast/south-central US: RMSF, ehrlichiosis; absent bite recall cannot exclude
Asplenia, older age, immunosuppression → severe babesiosis

rows.label: Clues
items: Fever, headache, myalgias; hypotension, confusion or organ failure → hospitalize
Persistent fever on doxycycline or disproportionate anemia → consider coinfection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Rickettsiae infect endothelium; Ehrlichia/Anaplasma infect leukocytes; Babesia infects RBCs
Borrelia spirochetes disseminate to skin, nervous system, heart, joints

rows.label: Dx
items: Early negative Lyme antibodies cannot exclude disease; isolated IgM after 30 days often misleading
★ **CBC, liver tests, creatinine**; anemia → hemolysis labs/smear; quantify babesial parasitemia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected **RMSF/ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis → doxycycline immediately**, including children; never await results
Erythema migrans → doxycycline 10 days or amoxicillin 14 days; arthritis → oral treatment 28 days
Lyme high-grade block/PR ≥300 ms → admit, IV ceftriaxone ± pacing; meningitis → doxycycline/ceftriaxone
★ **Babesia: atovaquone + azithromycin**; consider exchange for parasitemia >10%, severe hemolysis or organ failure

rows.label: Complications
items: RMSF: DIC/renal failure; Lyme: facial palsy; Babesia: ARDS, relapse in immunosuppressed patients

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **DEET/picaridin, permethrin clothing, tick checks**, prompt removal with tweezers
High-risk Lyme bite: endemic Ixodes, attached ≥36 hours → single doxycycline dose within 72 hours
No prophylaxis for rickettsial disease; no Lyme testing after asymptomatic bite

rows.label: Mimics
items: Viral syndrome: worsening illness/cytopenias still warrant tick evaluation
TTP: schistocytes rather than intraerythrocytic parasites
Septic arthritis: toxic monoarthritis → aspirate rather than presume Lyme

table.title: Pathogen signatures
rows: Expanding erythema migrans, not necessarily bullseye

urinary-tract-infections.name: Urinary tract infections
urinary-tract-infections.scope: Asymptomatic bacteriuria, acute cystitis, pyelonephritis, catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI), catheter removal, empiric antibiotics
urinary-tract-infections.core: Symptoms localize urinary infection: bladder disease lacks systemic illness; renal involvement causes fever or flank pain; bacteriuria alone is insufficient.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexual activity, spermicides, pregnancy, obstruction/stones, urinary retention, instrumentation
Catheter duration, diabetes, prior resistant isolates or antibiotics increase complicated-course risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort; absent vaginal discharge supports urinary source
★ **Rigors, CVA tenderness, vomiting, hypotension** → pyelonephritis or urosepsis
Catheterized patients: new urinary/systemic symptoms; cloudy urine or pyuria alone insufficient

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Usually ascending enteric bacteria, predominantly E coli; catheter biofilm maintains colonization
Urease-producing Proteus alkalinizes urine → struvite calculi and persistent infection
Pregnancy: progesterone ureteral relaxation + uterine compression → **stasis**; physiologic right-sided ureteral dilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urinalysis**: pyuria, leukocyte esterase, nitrites; pyelonephritis → heavy pyuria, WBC clumps/casts; negative nitrites don't exclude
Culture: pyelonephritis, pregnancy, CAUTI, recurrence/resistance; classic cystitis often clinical
Persistent fever after 48–72 hours, sepsis, or suspected obstruction → renal imaging
Asymptomatic bacteriuria: usually ≥100,000 CFU/mL; delirium alone → seek other causes without automatic antibiotics
Febrile non-toilet-trained child → **catheterized** urinalysis/culture; bag/clean-catch contaminate

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria only in pregnancy or before urologic mucosal trauma** in routine adult scenarios
★ CAUTI → **remove unnecessary catheter**; if needed and present >2 weeks, replace before culture/treatment
★ Infected obstructed collecting system → **urgent drainage + IV antibiotics**; antibiotics alone insufficient
Improving nonpregnant pyelonephritis: fluoroquinolone 5–7 days, other active drugs 7 days; high-risk cases individualized
Febrile infant → **cefotaxime/ceftriaxone**; first-generation cefazolin inadequate

rows.label: Complications
items: Bacteremia, septic shock, renal/perinephric abscess; pregnancy → preterm birth
Antibiotics → resistance, C difficile; fluoroquinolones → tendon injury, QT prolongation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid unnecessary catheters; closed drainage, daily removal assessment
Postmenopausal recurrence → vaginal estrogen
Recurrence ≥3/year or ≥2 in 6 months → postcoital or daily nitrofurantoin/TMP-SMX
Sporadic postcoital cystitis → **void before/after intercourse**; stop diaphragm/spermicide; condoms don't prevent

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vaginitis: discharge, pruritus, external burning
Urethritis: sexual exposure, discharge, positive gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT
Bladder pain syndrome: chronic symptoms, repeatedly negative cultures

table.title: Initial antibiotics; tailor to culture/resistance
rows: Ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin; initial ceftriaxone if resistance risk

valvular-heart-disease.name: Valvular heart disease
valvular-heart-disease.scope: Aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, physical exam, echocardiography, surgical and transcatheter replacement
valvular-heart-disease.core: Murmur timing, location, radiation, and loading maneuvers localize valve disease; symptoms and ventricular response determine intervention.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trileaflet calcification, age >70 → AS; rheumatic disease → MS
Bicuspid valve: murmur from youth, premature calcific AS (40s–60s); childhood **endocarditis**; adult aortic dissection
AR: endocarditis, dissection, **root dilation** (Marfan, hypertension; murmur along right sternal border)
MR: ischemia, myxomatous prolapse (connective tissue laxity), chamber dilation

rows.label: Clues
items: Exertional dyspnea, pulmonary edema, reduced exercise tolerance; abrupt deterioration suggests acute regurgitation
★ **Exertional syncope, angina, or HF** with obstruction → severe symptomatic disease
Squatting/handgrip increase regurgitant murmurs; standing/Valsalva → earlier MVP click, squatting → later

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Stenosis produces upstream pressure overload; regurgitation produces chamber volume overload
Acute regurgitation lacks compensatory dilation, rapidly elevating filling pressures and reducing forward output
Mitral stenosis: ↑LA pressure, ↑PCWP, ↑pulmonary artery pressure; **LVEDP normal**; AF abolishes presystolic accentuation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TTE Doppler** defines anatomy, severity, EF, chamber dimensions, pulmonary pressures
Severe AS: velocity ≥4 m/s, mean gradient ≥40, or valve area ≤1 cm²; discordance requires reassessment
Severe MS: valve area ≤1.5 cm²; TEE for thrombus before balloon intervention or uncertain anatomy
★ Acute murmur with shock → **urgent echocardiography**; TEE if endocarditis/dissection suspected

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute severe AR/MR → **urgent surgery**, stabilize with afterload reduction/diuresis if BP permits
Severe primary MR: **EF ≤60% or LVESD ≥40 mm** triggers intervention even without symptoms
Secondary MR → optimize HF treatment first; selected persistent severe cases benefit from transcatheter edge-to-edge repair
Avoid excessive preload reduction in severe AS; symptomatic relief never replaces needed valve intervention

rows.label: Complications
items: Heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, AF, systemic embolism, endocarditis
Mechanical prosthesis: thrombosis/bleeding; bioprosthesis: structural degeneration
Prosthetic dysfunction/paravalvular leak → new murmur, **schistocytes**, hemolytic anemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Warfarin for mechanical valves**; no DOAC substitution; rheumatic MS with AF also requires warfarin
Prosthetic valve or prior endocarditis → selected dental prophylaxis; native isolated MVP does not qualify
Periodic echo and symptom review; treat rheumatic fever to prevent recurrent valve injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: HCM: systolic murmur increases with Valsalva/standing
Aortic sclerosis: ejection murmur without significant gradient; flow murmur: normal valve anatomy

table.title: Valve signatures and definitive options
rows: Crescendo-decrescendo, carotids; soft A2; pulsus parvus et tardus
Early diastolic decrescendo; wide pulse pressure
Loud S1, opening snap, apical mid-diastolic rumble
Suitable symptomatic rheumatic valve → balloon commissurotomy
LLSB holosystolic, louder on inspiration; right HF
